record.title: Oral History Interview with Mike Morrow (part 4)

point.title: Dartmouth Mentorship and Returning from Cambodian Captivity
point.partial_transcript: Alright. This is Joanna Jou. Today is December 30th, 2025, and I am conducting part four of this oral history interview with Mr. Michael Morrow for the Dartmouth Vietnam Project.
point.synopsis: Morrow responds to a question about whether Dartmouth professor Ernie Young had CIA connections, saying he has no knowledge of such a link and instead remembers Young as a mentor who shaped his academic direction and helped facilitate his time in Taiwan. He then describes returning directly to Vietnam after being released from captivity in Cambodia, producing a series for Dispatch and the Washington Post network, honoring his promise not to return to Cambodia, and soon shifting toward Laos after being expelled from Vietnam.
point.keywords: Ernie Young; Dartmouth; Reischauer; Taiwan; Cambodia; Dispatch; Washington Post; Vietnam

point.title: Laos as a Neutral State and Hidden Theater of War
point.partial_transcript: What was your experience like there in Laos and covering?
point.synopsis: Morrow explains that Laos functioned under a nominally neutral political arrangement shaped by the Geneva Accords, with competing neutralist, conservative, and Pathet Lao factions. He emphasizes that the war in Laos could not be understood solely from inside Laos because American air and intelligence operations were deeply rooted across the Mekong in Thailand.
point.keywords: Laos; Geneva Accords; Pathet Lao; Vientiane; Mekong River; Thailand; Udon; Seventh Air Force; Air America

point.title: Intellectual Curiosity and Southeast Asia as an Unformed Field
point.partial_transcript: Yeah. I was just gonna ask what motivated you to, like, learn more about, like, the politics of what was going on in Thailand during this time when not many other journalists or news outlets were covering it?
point.synopsis: Morrow reflects on the intellectual curiosity that pushed him to investigate Thailand and Southeast Asia at a time when few journalists or academics were paying close attention. He connects this curiosity to Dartmouth, the loose boundaries of international relations as a field, and the appeal of Southeast Asia as an underdefined region where he could test ideas through direct reporting.
point.keywords: Dartmouth; Ernie Young; international relations; Southeast Asian studies; Timothy Allman; Laos; New York Times

point.title: Vietnam War Historiography and Anti-Imperialism
point.partial_transcript: Do you subscribe to a specific theory on Vietnam War historiography or different arguments that many historians have written about on American involvement or just the recollection of events of the Vietnam War, like domino theory and whatnot?
point.synopsis: Morrow discusses how his views on the Vietnam War evolved from realist and legalist frameworks rather than from organized anti-war activism or Marxist politics. He explains that his experience in Vietnam made him anti-imperialist, but not reflexively anti-American, and he applies that position to later critiques of Russian and Chinese imperial behavior as well.
point.keywords: Vietnam War historiography; domino theory; Hans Morgenthau; realism; anti-imperialism; anti-war movement; Noam Chomsky; Ukraine

point.title: Leaving Laos, Moving Through Thailand and Singapore, and Running a Magazine
point.partial_transcript: So after getting kicked out of Laos, did you move to Singapore, or was that later on?
point.synopsis: Morrow clarifies that he left Laos under threat rather than through formal expulsion, then continued reporting from Thailand while using Singapore as a base. He describes buying and running a petroleum magazine while continuing political reporting, creating a divided professional life between business journalism and radical regional analysis.
point.keywords: Laos; Northeast Thailand; Singapore; Southeast Asian Petroleum; Far Eastern Economic Review; freelance journalism; Dispatch

point.title: Singapore, Lee Kuan Yew, and Political Disillusionment
point.partial_transcript: And why, well, first, when, were you thrown out of Singapore and also why?
point.synopsis: Morrow describes initially viewing Singapore as a promising multicultural base for his Southeast Asia work. He then recounts becoming sharply critical of Lee Kuan Yew’s consolidation of power, restrictions on intellectual freedom, treatment of Malay culture, and covert international relationships.
point.keywords: Singapore; Lee Kuan Yew; multiculturalism; Malay culture; CIA activities; Israel; intellectual freedom

point.title: Malaysia, Hong Kong, and Regional Aftermath of Singapore Expulsion
point.partial_transcript: Where did you move after Singapore?
point.synopsis: After being expelled from Singapore, Morrow moves briefly to Johor Bahru and continues covering linked political movements in Malaysia and Singapore before Malaysian authorities also force him out. He relocates his petroleum magazine to Hong Kong, which becomes a base for covering Southeast Asia, India, Indonesia, and eventually China.
point.keywords: Johor Bahru; Malaysia; Kuala Lumpur; Singapore; Hong Kong; petroleum magazine; Southeast Asian politics

point.title: Postwar Vietnam Contacts and American Commercial Opening
point.partial_transcript: So did you go back to Vietnam and help with their oil and gas industry?
point.synopsis: Morrow recounts being contacted after the war by old acquaintances in Vietnam, including people he later understood had links to the revolutionary side, who wanted help rebuilding the economy. He describes joining the American Chamber of Commerce in Hong Kong and helping create a Vietnam Commercial Relations Committee modeled partly on earlier China commercial outreach.

point.title: Unofficial Missions to Hanoi and Opening Vietnam’s Oil Sector
point.partial_transcript: And so within a relatively short period of time, my friends and I, we were traveling to Hanoi a couple times a year on these, unofficial/official kind of missions, as guests of the Hanoi Chamber of Commerce.
point.synopsis: Morrow describes repeated unofficial visits to Hanoi as part of commercial outreach between Hong Kong-based American business figures and Vietnamese institutions. His petroleum background leads to meetings with Vietnamese oil officials, who seek American technical expertise and help building an oil industry not dominated solely by Soviet technology. Morrow then recounts how a promising effort to connect American petroleum expertise with Vietnam collapsed after an American official indirectly threatened the key technical expert. He describes the fallout inside the American Chamber of Commerce, including pressure to shut down the Vietnam committee and professional consequences for some of the bankers involved.

point.partial_transcript: And so they they retained me as a consultant. They gave me a little bit of money to go back to Vietnam to look for resort sites.
point.synopsis: Morrow describes a later effort by contacts in Saigon to bring him back as a consultant to help develop Vietnam’s tourism sector. He connects Saigon Tourism with the Mandarin Hotel Group and begins traveling along the Vietnamese coast looking for possible resort and hotel sites. Morrow then discusses running a Hong Kong publishing company, publishing an early Tiananmen photo book, and remaining connected to journalists covering major events in China and the Soviet bloc. point.title: Arrest in Da Nang and Interrogation in Saigon
point.partial_transcript: Anyway, I persuaded this guy, young fellow from Antwerp to come with me, go and look look at what was going on.
point.synopsis: Morrow recounts being detained in Da Nang with a potential investor after officials claim they lack the proper travel permit. He is transported back to Saigon, separated from the investor, placed in a holding cell, and interrogated for weeks as an alleged CIA agent. Morrow later interprets his detention within a wider political shift inside the Vietnamese Communist Party after Tiananmen and the collapse of Soviet communism. He says many of his Vietnamese contacts were purged or imprisoned, and he was eventually released after intervention from Kraisak Choonhavan, after which he abandoned hopes of working in Vietnam.

point.title: Hong Kong, Illness, Divorce, and Personal Reckoning
point.partial_transcript: So did you go back to Hong Kong after leaving Vietnam?
point.synopsis: Morrow describes returning to Hong Kong after Vietnam, a period marked by personal instability, marital collapse, illness, and temporary paralysis from an exotic virus. He reflects on his relationships, his children, and the gradual process by which illness and aging forced him to reconsider the destructive pace of his life.
point.keywords: Hong Kong; Vancouver; illness; paralysis; divorce; family; Thailand; TongPan; children

point.title: Publishing Crisis and the Opening of Shenzhen

He describes Shenzhen’s transformation from a small border area into a city filled with trading companies tied to inland Chinese provinces and municipalities seeking direct access to foreign markets. Morrow describes a fast-paced trading routine built around multiple daily trips between Hong Kong and Shenzhen, exploiting communication gaps before phone and travel systems improved. He works with Indian, Korean, Japanese, and Chinese contacts, moving from small trade deals into textiles, metals, and ferrosilicon.
point.keywords: Hong Kong publishing; digital transition; Shenzhen; Deng Xiaoping; oyster commune; trading companies; telephone lines

point.synopsis: Morrow recounts meeting a well-connected Chinese businesswoman who draws him into larger-scale metals trading backed by elite political networks. Her family history, Cultural Revolution experience, and access to capital reveal how Deng-era commercial openings relied on trusted pre-Cultural Revolution relationships and political privilege. Morrow describes helping open a South African iron ore supply route to China during the apartheid era, before formal diplomatic relations made such trade straightforward. point.title: Exit from Metals Trading and Digital Publishing Pivot
point.partial_transcript: Sumitomo had come looking for me for selling bogus goods. Fortunately, it was a very small shipment. And they let me go, but it ruined my business with Sumitomo.
point.synopsis: Morrow reflects on the financial losses and risks in large-scale commodity trading, including stolen shipments, sunken cargo, and thin margins. After a powerful Hong Kong partner threatens him, he concludes he is too close to both organized crime and Chinese state-linked capital and exits the business. Morrow describes bringing his brother into the China trading business, which leads to selling fiberglass manufacturing equipment into China and eventually becomes his brother’s successful enterprise. He then pivots into digital publishing, winning a contract to digitize the Far Eastern Economic Review archive despite initially lacking the technical infrastructure to do so.

point.title: Digitizing the Far Eastern Economic Review and Early Digital Publishing

The success gives him credibility in digital publishing and leads to additional projects, including early interface work for the South China Morning Post. Morrow describes meeting Silicon Valley entrepreneurs developing language-learning technology based on speech recognition and data analysis. point.title: Founding a Mongolia Company and Moving to Mongolia

When the U.S. company decides to close the Mongolian subsidiary, Morrow buys it personally rather than see it written off as a failed idea. He moves to Mongolia hoping to develop a new business, but the Crimea crisis and Russia’s recentralization quickly undermine his Siberian education-technology strategy.
point.keywords: Mongolia; foreign investment law; Ulaanbaatar; Siberia; Yakutia; Buryatia; education technology; subsidiary; Mongolia subsidiary; retirement; Silicon Valley company; Crimea; Putin; education sector

This becomes the basis for his effort to build a Mongolian cheesemaking movement, later including a restaurant, agro hub, and broader projects despite financial fragility and COVID setbacks.

He links his difficulties with intimacy, restlessness, and self-isolation to the psychological effects of Vietnam and concludes by describing his current attempts to rebuild forms of family connection late in life.
